title: What We Need to Know About EdTech, Data, and Privacy
author: First Fish Chronicles
summary: Emily of First Fish Chronicles presents a comprehensive FAQ arguing that EdTech companies should be understood as a for-profit industry structurally misaligned with healthy child development: 'EdTech is just Big Tech in a sweater vest.' The FAQ covers: how EdTech products pervade schools (hundreds to thousands per district); why data collection harms children (student records worth $250-350 on the black market, 96% of EdTech tools sharing data with third parties, 'anonymized' data routinely re-identified by identity-resolution firms); and why blanket 'User Agreements' do not constitute legally valid informed parental consent. A September 2025 FTC amicus brief is a key enforcement development: it established that schools can no longer stand in for parents in consenting to EdTech data collection under COPPA, invalidating the consent structure most EdTech companies have relied upon. Concrete harms catalogued include: law enforcement using behavioral records to predict future criminal behavior, targeted ads with dangerous content, and data breaches (the PowerSchool breach leaked 70 million records across 40+ years). The article closes with the author's own experience successfully opting her daughter out of the school-issued Chromebook for two years, and with the four questions schools must be required to answer before adopting any EdTech product.
points: 96% of EdTech tools share children's personal information with third parties -- the industry's success metric is 'time on device,' which is structurally opposed to healthy child development and puts the business model in direct conflict with children's interests.

A student's data record is worth $250-350 on the black market; across 50 million U.S. schoolchildren that represents approximately $15 billion in data -- explaining why EdTech is already a $205B industry projected to reach $800B in the next decade.

Anonymized EdTech data is not actually anonymous: identity-resolution firms routinely reverse-engineer anonymized datasets to re-identify individual students, making the privacy assurances schools give parents legally and practically unfounded.

The September 2025 FTC amicus brief established that schools cannot legally stand in for parents in consenting to EdTech data collection under COPPA -- a foundational shift that invalidates the consent structure most of the industry has relied upon.

The four questions schools must demand answers to before adopting any EdTech product: Is it effective? Is it safe? Is it legal? Is it superior to a human teacher? -- and currently the honest answer to all four is No.
quotes: EdTech, like Big Tech, is an industry. EdTech, like Big Tech, is in this for profit, not children. EdTech is just Big Tech in a sweater vest.

The erosion of privacy rights is the first step in the erosion of other rights. EVEN IF we as adults are knowingly consenting to all the data collection going on in our digital lives... children are minors who cannot legally consent.
Internet Safety Labs found that 96% of EdTech tools share children's personal information with third parties.
The United States Department of Education found that one student data record is worth between $250 and $350 on the black market. There are nearly 50 million school-aged children in the United States.

Many of those 'User Agreements' that schools require parents to sign at the start of the school year say nothing about the school's responsibility to protect student data... If the document doesn't say anything about what happens when your child is harmed on a school-issued device, then the 'agreement' is not there to protect your child.
This amicus brief establishes that schools can no longer stand in the shoes of parents for the purpose of consenting to data collection.

There are four questions we must insist schools answer before providing children access to EdTech products: Is this effective? Is this safe? Is this legal? Is this superior to a human teacher? Until and unless the answer to all four questions must be a resounding Yes. Currently, it is a terrifying No.
